author: world today news
title: High-Sensitivity Troponin: A Breakthrough in Primary Prevention?
text:
Could troponin assays revolutionize primary cardiovascular disease (CVD) prevention? A recent study explores how integrating high-sensitivity cardiac troponin assays into existing risk models could considerably enhance our ability to identify individuals at risk.discover how this innovative approach could reshape treatment decisions and improve patient outcomes by learning about the role of troponin assays in early CVD detection and prevention.
Troponin assays: A New Tool in Primary CVD Prevention? A recent meta-analysis suggests that incorporating high-sensitivity cardiac troponin assays into existing risk-prediction models could significantly enhance primary prevention efforts for cardiovascular disease (CVD).
Published in the April 15, 2025, issue of the Journal of the American College of Cardiology , the study explores the potential of these assays, traditionally used for diagnosing myocardial infarction (MI), to identify individuals at risk even at very low concentrations of cardiac troponin T and I.
Repurposing Troponin: A Proactive Approach The study’s authors propose a novel approach: repurposing troponin assays, leveraging their existing accessibility and affordability for broader prognostic applications. Spencer J. Keene, PhD, from the University of Cambridge, England, a joint frist author of the paper, emphasizes this potential.
Keene told TCTMD that the data support maybe more use and also educating clinicians about using them in a different way. This shift could refine risk stratification and inform treatment decisions, particularly for those on the borderline of statin initiation .
The Impact on Treatment Decisions While high-sensitivity troponin assays may not drastically alter treatment for patients already identified as high-risk, they could significantly influence the management of individuals at low or intermediate risk. Keene elaborates:
We would still probably prefer that the high-risk group gets statins. The first step is that people should use risk-prediction models to support their decision-making,and then the next step would be looking at these add-on factors that could also support decision-making if there’s some uncertainty.
Spencer J. Keene, phd, University of Cambridge
Expert Commentary: Integrating Troponins into Guidelines Dr. Nicholas Marston from Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston, MA, concurs that troponin assays have less utility for patients already meeting statin therapy criteria. However,he highlights the evolving landscape of risk assessment:
Current guidelines support the use of risk enhancers to help guide that discussion and make a decision about statins. Currently those are high-sensitivity CRP, eGFR for chronic kidney disease, [and] family history of early heart disease—these might be things that kind of push you over to starting statins in a patient. And I think high-sensitivity troponins could be one of those as well.
nicholas Marston, MD, Brigham and Women’s Hospital
These “risk enhancers” can provide additional details to refine treatment strategies.
CAPRICE study: Key Findings The CAPRICE study, a cornerstone of this research, analyzed data from 62,150 adults without known CVD. Key details include:
Mean age: 61 years Female depiction: 48.5% High-sensitivity cardiac troponin T (hs-cTnT) measured in 50,523 participants (median concentration: 5.0 ng/L) High-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTnI) used in 28,090 participants (median concentration: 3.3 ng/L) Over a median follow-up of 11.8 years for hs-cTnT and 9.8 years for hs-cTnI, notable findings emerged:
First onset CVD events (coronary heart disease or stroke) occurred in 16.1% (hs-cTnT) and 13.3% (hs-cTnI) of patients. Risk increased with each standard deviation higher concentration of hs-cTnT (HR 1.31; 95% CI 1.25-1.37) and hs-cTnI (HR 1.26; 95% CI 1.19-1.33). Adding troponin assays to conventional risk factors improved overall predictive accuracy. Researchers estimated that hs-cTnT and hs-cTnI screening could prevent one additional CVD event for every 408 and 473 individuals without known CVD,respectively,by reclassifying them to high risk and initiating statin therapy.
Troponin T vs. Troponin I: A Comparative Analysis Keene noted the surprising similarity in risk prediction enhancement between the two troponin assays, with hs-cTnT showing a slight advantage over hs-cTnI. He addressed the existing debate:
There has been some controversy around whether or not troponin I or troponin T is better. I think a lot of clinicians prefer troponin I and thought that it was a better prognostic marker than troponin T, and we essentially found that they’re either similar or even that troponin T is better.
Spencer J. Keene, PhD, University of Cambridge
Challenges and Future Directions Despite the promising findings, Keene cautions against using troponin levels to deny statins to high-risk individuals. He identifies key obstacles to wider adoption:
Physician awareness Cost barriers in lower-resourced areas Further research is needed to confirm these findings and assess cost-effectiveness.
A Shift in Clinical Thinking An accompanying editorial by Cian P. McCarthy, MBBCh, from Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, and colleagues, highlights the potential benefits of incorporating hs-cTn into CVD risk-based primary treatment allocation. This approach could increase the number of CVD events prevented and reduce overtreatment in lower-risk individuals.
However, McCarthy et al. emphasize that this requires a significant mindset shift for clinicians , who primarily associate troponin assays with MI diagnosis.
Workflow Integration and Future Research Marston points out that current institutional software often flags high-sensitivity troponin assays ordered in stable patients, reflecting the need for workflow adjustments to accommodate broader use outside acute settings.
He advocates for studies demonstrating the direct impact of troponin levels on treatment outcomes, similar to the JUPITER trial for high-sensitivity C-reactive protein. Physicians really want to see that it can impact management and patient outcomes, Marston added.
Key Takeaways High-sensitivity cardiac troponin assays may improve CVD risk prediction. These assays could refine treatment decisions, especially for intermediate-risk patients. Wider adoption requires a shift in clinical thinking and workflow adjustments. Further research is needed to confirm findings and assess cost-effectiveness.
